planting.note: Mount a rooted pup on a slab of tree fern fiber or cork with sphagnum moss backing in spring so new roots can establish through the warm, humid months before winter.

directions: This Southeast Asian epiphyte produces two distinct frond types: rounded, overlapping shield fronds that clasp its mount and build a basket of trapped debris, and dramatically long, strap-like fertile fronds that hang and fork repeatedly as they age. Mount it on bark or in a wire basket with sphagnum rather than potting it in soil, and let the mount dry between thorough waterings. Give it bright, filtered light under taller canopy and high humidity, since direct sun scorches the fronds while deep shade yields leggy, weak growth. Mature specimens are prized for the sheer length of their pendulous fertile fronds, which can eventually trail several feet.

planting.note: Attach a pup to a bark slab or hang it in a basket in spring, backing the roots with sphagnum moss so it establishes before the plant is moved indoors for winter.

directions: Native to mainland Southeast Asia, this staghorn was long confused with the superficially similar Platycerium grande of Australia and New Guinea before being recognized as its own species. Upright, antler-like fertile fronds are covered in a dense, felty brown indumentum when young that helps the plant handle brighter light and occasional dry spells better than many of its relatives. Grow it mounted or basketed with excellent drainage around the roots, water thoroughly then allow the mount to dry, and keep humidity moderate to high. Its broad basal shield fronds overlap like roof shingles and should never be trimmed away, since they are the plant's main water- and nutrient-catching structure.

planting.note: Mount this small species on a light, well-draining slab in spring and let it dry noticeably between waterings, since it is adapted to Madagascar's seasonally dry forests rather than constant rainforest humidity.

directions: This diminutive Madagascar endemic is one of the smallest staghorn ferns in cultivation, with narrow fertile fronds that fork into four divisions rather than the broad antler shapes typical of the genus. Its native habitat is drier and more seasonal than that of most Platycerium, so it tolerates brighter light and more thorough drying between waterings than relatives like P. bifurcatum. Mount it on a small bark or cork slab with minimal moss so air can reach the roots quickly after watering. Its compact size makes it well suited to collections where larger staghorns would outgrow the space.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into crevices of a shaded rock wall or trough in spring, using a gritty, humus-rich mix that drains quickly but holds some moisture.

directions: Native to Australian rock crevices and open woodland, this small fern earns its common name from the way its narrow fronds trail outward in a chain of small, fan-shaped segments, occasionally rooting at the tip to form new plantlets. Rather than growing upright, it drapes over rock ledges and fallen logs, making it a good choice tucked into a shaded wall or stone trough. It prefers gritty, well-drained soil with some organic matter and resents being waterlogged, so site it where water moves through quickly. Give it dappled shade and modest but regular moisture, and it will slowly knit itself into crevices over several seasons.

planting.note: Mount on bark or pot in an open, bark-based fern mix in spring, keeping it in a hanging basket or on a vertical mount so the fronds can drape freely.

directions: In its native New Zealand and southeastern Australian forests, this fern grows as an epiphyte on tree trunks and rock faces, sending down long, leathery, deeply cut fronds that hang and sway rather than standing upright. It does best mounted on bark or grown in a hanging basket of chunky, free-draining fern mix, since the thick fronds are adapted to brief periods of drying between rain. Keep it in deep, humid shade similar to a forest understory and avoid letting the roots sit wet, which encourages rot more readily than drought. Its pendulous habit makes it a striking specimen for a shaded porch or greenhouse rather than a typical upright houseplant fern.

planting.note: Plant divisions or bulbil-grown plantlets in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, shaded bed or container.

directions: This compact selection of the New Zealand mother fern stays denser and darker green than the typical species, with finely divided, lacy fronds that arch from a central crown. Like its parent species, mature fronds carry small bulbils along their surface that can be pegged onto moist potting mix to root into new plantlets, making propagation simple without division. Grow it in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, shaded spot protected from wind and hard frost, since the fronds brown quickly in dry air or cold exposure. Its tidy habit suits shaded containers and understory plantings where the species itself would sprawl larger.
